[[Image:Robert W. Brooks.jpg|thumb|right|alt=Robert W. Brooks (1985)|Robert W. Brooks (1985)]]
'''Robert Wolfe Brooks''' (September 16, 1952 &ndash; September 5, 2002) was an American [[mathematician]] known for his work in [[spectral geometry]], [[Riemann surfaces]], [[circle packing]]s, and [[differential geometry]].

==Biography==
Brooks was born in 1952 in [[Washington, D.C.]] and grew up in [[Bethesda, Maryland]], where he graduated in 1970 from [[Walt Whitman High School (Maryland)|Walt Whitman High School]]. In 1974 he completed his Masters thesis from [[Harvard University]];<ref name="WPObituary">{{cite news |title=Robert Brooks |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2002/09/19/robert-brooks/050b21c6-3d5e-41fc-a1fd-f6f461e3a9d3/ |access-date=April 9, 2025 |work=The Washington Post |date=September 19, 2002}}</ref> his thesis "[[Bertrand Russell|Russell]], [[Henri Poincaré|Poincaré]], and the foundations of geometry" won him the [[Bowdoin Prizes|Bowdoin Prize]] for Essays in the Natural Sciences in 1975.<ref>{{cite web |title=Russell, Poincaré, and the foundations of geometry |url=https://id.lib.harvard.edu/alma/990046901320203941/catalog |website=Harvard Library |access-date=April 9, 2025}}</ref>

He received his [[Ph.D.]] from Harvard University in 1977; his thesis, ''The smooth cohomology of groups of diffeomorphisms'', was written under the supervision of [[Raoul Bott]]. He then undertook [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral studies]] with J. Peter Matelski at the [[Stony Brook University|State University of New York at Stony Brook]], where they created pictures of fractals, leading to [[Benoit Mandelbrot]]'s creation of the [[Mandelbrot set]] in 1980.<ref name="WPObituary" />

He worked at the [[University of Maryland]] (1979&ndash;1984), then at the [[University of Southern California]], and then, from 1995, at the [[Technion]] in [[Haifa]].<ref name="WPObituary" /><ref name=buser>{{cite book|mr=2179784|last=Buser|first=Peter|authorlink=Jürg Peter Buser|chapter=On the mathematical work of Robert Brooks| title=Geometry, spectral theory, groups, and dynamics|pages=1&ndash;35|series=Contemp. Math.|volume=387|publisher=Amer. Math. Soc.|location=Providence, RI|year=2005|isbn=9780821885642|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=S9fCX9j_JPwC&q=On+the+mathematical+work+of+Robert+Brooks&pg=PA1}}</ref>

Brooks died from [[Myocardial infarction|heart attack]] during a visit to [[Montreal, Canada]] and was buried in Sde Yehoshua cemetery in Haifa.<ref>{{cite web |title=ברוקס רוברט ראובן |url=https://kdh.org.il/regular-serch/search-results-deceased/grave-info/?deceased=59509 |website=Hevra Kadisha Haifa |access-date=April 9, 2025}}</ref> He was survived by his parents David and Harriet Brooks, his wife Sharon and four children.<ref name="WPObituary" /> His eldest son [[Shimon Brooks]] is a mathematics professor at [[Bar-Ilan University]].

==Work==
In an influential paper {{harv|Brooks|1981}}, Brooks proved that the [[bounded cohomology]] of a [[topological space]] is [[isomorphic]] to the bounded cohomology of its [[fundamental group]].<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Journal of Mathematical Sciences|volume=37|issue=3|pages=1090&ndash;1115|doi=10.1007/BF01086634|mr=0806562| title=Foundations of the theory of bounded cohomology|first=Nikolai V.|last=Ivanov|year=1987|s2cid=122503635|authorlink=Nikolai V. Ivanov}}</ref>
